newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-UK's current account surplus best in 9 years.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-UK's current account surplus best in 9 years.

text.p: Britain had its largest current account surplus for nine years in the second quarter of 1996 and its overall annual economic growth rate was revised up to 2.2 percent, the Office for National Statistics said on Tuesday.

Official interest rates were left unchanged at 5.75 percent after Monday's monetary policy meeting between Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Kenneth Clarke and Bank of England Governor Eddie George.

The current account deficit for the second quarter showed an unexpected 457 million pound ($712 million) surplus after a deficit of 786 million in the first quarter. Financial markets had expected a second quarter deficit of around 1.2 billion pounds.

"This improvement was largely due to record surpluses on trade in services and investment income," the statistics office said. The current account surplus was the first for over a year and the largest since the first quarter of 1987.
Gross domestic product (GDP) grew 0.5 percent in the second quarter, up from the 0.4 percent growth government statisticians had previously reported.
Annual GDP growth was now put at 2.2 percent compared with the previous estimate of 1.8 percent.
"The figures show a healthy and sustainable economic performance," Treasury minister Angela Knight said.

City economists said the figures added fuel to Bank of England Governor Eddie George's argument that interest rates should be raised to counter the risk of a future resurgence in inflation as the economy gathers steam.
"Monetary policy is clearly too loose," said Kevin Gardiner, an economist at Morgan Stanley.

The central bank conducted routine money market operations at unchanged interest rates on Tuesday morning, indicating that Clarke, who has the final say on monetary policy, had ordered no change in official rates at Monday's policy meeting.

The Chancellor has cut rates four times since December and, with a general election due by May 1997, is clearly reluctant to raise them again. He overruled the Bank of England's call at the July monetary meeting for rates to be raised to six percent.
"The debate will now clearly shift from possible rate cuts to whether the government can resist pressure for a rate rise before the general election," said Ian Stewart, UK economist at Merrill Lynch.
A breakdown of the balance of payments figures showed a surplus on investment income in the second quarter of 3.7 billion pounds, the highest figure on record.
Services showed a surplus of 1.9 billion pounds while trade in goods showed a marginally lower deficit of 3.6 billion.
The revised GDP figures showed construction and a broad range of service industries growing much faster than previously thought.
Alex Garrard, an economist at UBS, said recent buoyancy in retailing and signs of recovery in manufacturing suggested economic growth would pick up in the coming months.
"With only subdued inflation left in Clarke's stock of feasible excuses, further rate cuts are almost certainly off the agenda for the time being," he said. ($1=.6420 Pound)
